title: This syllable is Brahman
theme: This syllable is Brahman, this syllable is the highest; whoever knows this syllable has whatever he desires.

words.context: Śaṅkara: the higher Brahman; Raṅgarāmānuja: «जप्येषु ध्येयेषु च श्रेष्ठम्»
Śaṅkara: «उपास्य ब्रह्मेति», having meditated on it as Brahman

sandhi.rule: etat before h becomes etad, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते), and the h after d may become dh, P. 8.4.62 (झयो होऽन्यतरस्याम्). hi + eva give hy eva, P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि); eva + akṣaram join long, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः).

sandhi.type: aḥ before a voiced consonant; t voiced
sandhi.rule: yaḥ before y becomes yo, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च) and P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः); yat before a vowel becomes yad, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते).

sandhi_exceptions.note: The base prints brahma etad unjoined at the pāda boundary, as Śaṅkara’s and Raṅgarāmānuja’s quotations of the verse do; Madhva’s text joins brahmaitad (corrections.json). Unjoined, each pāda counts eight syllables.

morphology.note: ‘Imperishable’ (a- with √kṣar ‘flow away’) and ‘syllable’: the verse uses both senses at once. Śaṅkara: the syllable is the symbol of both Brahmans, «तयोर्हि प्रतीकमेतदक्षरम्».

translation.literal: This syllable alone indeed [is] Brahman; this syllable alone indeed [is] the highest. Having known this syllable alone indeed, whoever desires whatever — his [is] that.
translation.readable: This syllable is Brahman; this syllable is the highest. Whoever knows this syllable will have whatever they desire.

anvaya: एतत् हि एव अक्षरम् ब्रह्म, एतत् हि एव अक्षरम् परम् । एतत् हि एव अक्षरम् ज्ञात्वा यः यत् इच्छति, तस्य तत् [भवति] ।
syntax: Three statements, each opening etad dhy evākṣaram. The first two are nominal sentences (‘this syllable is Brahman’, ‘this syllable is the highest’). The third has an absolutive (jñātvā) inside a relative clause (yo yad icchati), and the main clause tasya tat (‘his is that’) leaves ‘be’ to be supplied.

ambiguities.topic: brahma … param: two Brahmans or one?
ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara supplies ‘lower’ to the first statement: «एतद्ध्येवाक्षरं ब्रह्म अपरम् एतद्ध्येवाक्षरं परं च» — the syllable is the symbol of both the lower and the higher Brahman, so that one who meditates on it attains whichever he seeks: the higher is to be known, «परं चेत् ज्ञातव्यम्», the lower to be reached, «अपरं चेत् प्राप्तव्यम्». Raṅgarāmānuja: the syllable is called Brahman because it is the means of reaching Brahman — «ब्रह्मप्राप्तिसाधनत्वात् ब्रह्म» — and ‘highest’ means best among what is recited and meditated on: «जप्येषु ध्येयेषु च श्रेष्ठम् इत्यर्थः».

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: Anuṣṭubh, 16 + 16, regular. The hiatus brahma etad falls at the boundary of the first two pādas and keeps each at eight; Madhva’s joined brahmaitad would count fifteen for the line.

beginner: Having named the goal as Om, Death now praises the syllable itself. The Sanskrit word for syllable also means imperishable, and the verse uses both meanings at once: this syllable, this imperishable thing, is Brahman, the ultimate reality, and it is the highest. Whoever truly knows it receives whatever they seek. Śaṅkara explains the double statement carefully. There is a higher and a lower form of Brahman, and Om is the symbol of both. Someone who meditates on Om seeking the highest comes to know it; someone seeking the lower attains that. Raṅgarāmānuja says the syllable is called Brahman because it is the means by which Brahman is reached, and it is the highest of all things to recite and meditate on. Madhva cites a verse that names the imperishable as Viṣṇu.
analogy: Like a key that is also the name of the house it opens.

commentary.q: What does Death say of the syllable?
commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That this syllable is Brahman and the highest, and that whoever knows it has whatever they desire.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: «एतद्ध्येवाक्षरं ब्रह्म अपरम् एतद्ध्येवाक्षरं परं च । तयोर्हि प्रतीकमेतदक्षरम्» — the syllable is the symbol of both the lower and the higher Brahman. Knowing it means meditating on it as Brahman, «उपास्य ब्रह्मेति»; then what one seeks follows: the higher is to be known, «परं चेत् ज्ञातव्यम्», the lower to be reached.

commentary.q: Raṅgarāmānuja: the word that names Brahman
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: In this verse and the next Death praises the word that names Brahman: «एवं वाचकं प्रणवं द्वाभ्यां मन्त्राभ्यां स्तौति». It is called Brahman as the means to Brahman, «ब्रह्मप्राप्तिसाधनत्वात् ब्रह्म», and is the highest among things recited and meditated on, «जप्येषु ध्येयेषु च श्रेष्ठम् इत्यर्थः». One who meditates on it wishing for a fruit receives that fruit.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Madhva’s whole comment on 1.2.14–17 is a verse he cites without naming its source («इति च»): «एतद्ध्येवाक्षरं ब्रह्म विष्ण्वाख्यं परमव्ययम्» — ‘this imperishable Brahman, called Viṣṇu, highest, unchanging’.

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: The base, Śaṅkara’s quotation of the verse and Raṅgarāmānuja write brahma etad apart; Madhva’s text joins brahmaitad (corrections.json). The hiatus stands at the pāda boundary.

advaita.text: Om is the symbol (pratīka) of both the lower and the higher Brahman: «तयोर्हि प्रतीकमेतदक्षरम्».

visistadvaita.text: Om is called Brahman as the means to it — «ब्रह्मप्राप्तिसाधनत्वात् ब्रह्म» — and is the best support of recitation and meditation.

dvaita.text: The imperishable is Viṣṇu, on a verse Madhva cites: «विष्ण्वाख्यं परमव्ययम्».

schools.disagreement: Śaṅkara distinguishes a higher and a lower Brahman, both symbolised by Om; Raṅgarāmānuja and Madhva know one Brahman, the Lord, whom Om names and through whom meditation finds its support.

parallels.quote: एतद्वै सत्यकाम परं चापरं च ब्रह्म यदोङ्कारः
parallels.note: The Praśna: Om is the higher and the lower Brahman — the distinction Śaṅkara reads here.
The Gītā: Om, the one syllable, is Brahman.

parallels.quote: ॐ इत्य् एतद् अक्षरम् इदं सर्वं
parallels.note: The Māṇḍūkya opens with the same syllable: ‘Om — this syllable is all this’.

contemporary.text: The verse gives its whole weight to a single syllable. In a day of thousands of words, most of them read and forgotten, it is worth noticing what it would mean to give that kind of attention to one. This is a reflection, not a claim made by the text.

reflect.beginner: Is there a word that means far more to you than its dictionary meaning?
reflect.deeper: Why might the verse say both ‘Brahman’ and ‘the highest’? Does Śaṅkara’s distinction between a higher and a lower Brahman help, or does it make the verse say less than it seems to?
reflect.practice: Choose one word that names what you most value and put it somewhere you will see it each day.

flags.note: Madhva’s text joins brahmaitad; AS, Śaṅkara and Raṅgarāmānuja print the hiatus (corrections.json; orthographic).
brahma … param: the lower and the higher Brahman (Śaṅkara), or one Brahman (Raṅgarāmānuja, Madhva).
